title: Prompting with Respect: Cultural Norms and User Experience in LLM Interactions
authors: Sujin Yang, Seoyoung Oh, Ha Eun Shim
abstract: Despite growing interest in prompt engineering, its influence on user experience—particularly in relation to cultural communication norms—remains largely unexplored. This controlled experiment examined how respectful versus directive prompting—a culturally meaningful contrast in Korean—affects Korean users’ psychological experience during LLM interactions. Forty-three Korean female college students were randomly assigned to respectful prompt (RP) (using polite requests, compliments, and gratitude) or directive prompt (DP) (using imperatives, criticism, and performance-based penalties) conditions. Participants completed a writing task using ChatGPT. Results indicated that RPs yielded significantly higher satisfaction, particularly for affinity and likability, whereas the difference in perceived output quality was smaller and nonsignificant. Furthermore, RPs elicited socially supportive ChatGPT responses, whereas DPs were followed by apologies, suggesting bidirectional social adaptation between users and ChatGPT. Together, these findings suggest that culturally grounded communicative conventions may shape users’ subjective experience even where perceived output quality does not differ significantly, pointing to culturally adaptive large language model systems that recognize diverse communication patterns as essential design considerations rather than imposing universal paradigms.

title: Antecedents and consequences of face filter use on social media: the role of use frequency and depth
authors: Jingjing Tong, Chunyi Xian, Jingjun (David) Xu
abstract: Purpose Face filters are pervasive in selfie-based social media practices, raising concerns about their psychological implications. This study examines the social drivers of face-filter use frequency and depth, their positive and negative psychological consequences and how these two dimensions jointly shape user outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-discrepancy theory (SDT), we conceptualize descriptive and subjective norms as self-guides influencing two dimensions of filter use: frequency (which regulates discrepancy accessibility) and depth (which regulates discrepancy availability). We propose a model linking filter use to affective outcomes and self-evaluations and examine the interactive effects of use frequency and depth on these outcomes. The model was tested using survey data from 328 participants. Findings Descriptive and subjective norms positively predict use frequency and depth. Use frequency, but not use depth, increases self-confidence by enhancing appearance self-esteem; whereas both frequency and depth increase negative moods by amplifying self-discrepancy perceptions. Additionally, the interaction between use frequency and depth is positively associated with both appearance self-esteem and perceived self-discrepancy. Originality/value This study is among the first to integrate SDT and social norms to explain the antecedents and dual consequences of face-filter use. By distinguishing use frequency and depth as two self-regulation dimensions in digital self-presentation, this study highlights their main and interactive effects on positive and negative psychological outcomes and clarifies the underlying mechanisms.

title: Economic Conditions, Public Sentiment, and News Coverage: A Time-Series Analysis of Economic Agenda Dynamics in South Korea
authors: Sei-Hill Kim, Wansoo Lee
abstract: Drawing on 23 years of economic news in South Korea, this study investigates how key economic indicators interact with the volume and tone of economic news, which can both shape and reflect public opinion, particularly the public’s economic sentiment. Time-series analyses revealed that unfavorable economic conditions, reflected in lower Stock Market Index and GDP growth rates as well as higher Consumer Price Index (CPI) and unemployment rates, were associated with greater news coverage of these topics in the subsequent month. The tone of news coverage was largely unrelated to economic indicators, suggesting that the overall news sentiment may not closely align with real-world economic conditions. Finally, the relationship between economic news and public sentiment was reciprocal rather than one-directional. Implications for economic journalism are discussed in detail.

title: Building Deep Data Through Screens: Princeton-SMART for Mobile Communication Research
authors: Jihye Lee, Kentaro Oriuchi, Daniel Muise, Jacob N. Shapiro
abstract: This article introduces Princeton-SMART, open-source screen-capture software designed to generate deep data on mobile communication behavior. Princeton-SMART unobtrusively collects screenshots and on-screen text from Android devices at short intervals in naturalistic settings. We describe a research pipeline for secure data collection, preprocessing, and analysis, drawing on over 1.5 million screenshots contributed by U.S. job seekers over 6 weeks. We demonstrate how job-search activities can be identified using vision-language AI models and methodological considerations encountered during the process. We conclude by discussing opportunities and practical implications for integrating Princeton-SMART into mobile communication research.

title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
authors: Carlos Entrena-Serrano, Trisha Meyer, Emilia Gómez, Jo Pierson
abstract: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.

title: Understanding the Effects of Message Complexity and Epistemic Uncertainty on Attitudinal, Cognitive, and Behavioral Responses to Messages About Microplastics
authors: Zhuling Liu, Xiaodong Yang
abstract: This study examined how message complexity and epistemic uncertainty affect attitudes toward science, information overload, and behavioral intention using a 2 × 2 factorial design. Although no main effects were detected, the interaction between complexity and uncertainty on information overload depended on intolerance of uncertainty (IU): uncertainty reduced information overload for low-IU individuals but increased it for high-IU individuals. Moreover, the conditional indirect effect of uncertainty on behavioral intention through information overload was significant under high message complexity at specific levels of IU. When message complexity was low, this indirect effect was not significant at any level of IU.

title: The Effects of Online Harassment of Scientists on Bystander Scientists
authors: Jana Laura Egelhofer, Christina Seeger, Alice Binder
abstract: Scientists who share research on social media increasingly face harassment, which is visible to many bystanders, including other scientists. We report a preregistered experiment testing how exposure to such harassment affects bystander scientists ( N = 846). Drawing on social identity approaches, we argue that bystander scientists may react similarly to directly targeted scientists. Results show that exposure to harassment increases anxiety and risk perceptions but does not reduce willingness to engage in science communication; it slightly increases perceived trustworthiness of targeted scientists. Presumed influence shapes some of these effects. Shifting attention to bystanders, we highlight broader societal consequences of harassment against scientists.

title: It Doesn’t Take Extremes to Trigger Hate: A Mixed-Methods Study on Meme Extremity and User Comments on 9GAG
authors: Antonia Drexel, Ursula Kristin Schmid
abstract: Users engage with socially and politically relevant topics by sharing memes and adopting the creative styles of meme-sharing platforms like 9GAG. Although memes can contain political critique, research also linked them to hate speech and increasingly extreme content. Little attention has been paid to entertainment-first platforms, where (perceived) homogeneity, anonymity, and humor-driven social norms may shape how political and hateful content is produced and discussed in the comment section. This study addresses this gap using a sequential mixed-methods design. First, we analyzed 343 memes on 9GAG with quantitative content analysis, categorizing them into classes based on varying degrees of extreme content using latent class analysis. Second, via qualitative content analysis, we investigated the comment sections of six memes representing each identified class to determine how extreme content levels influence hateful comments. Results show that anonymity and ingroup identity foster a climate in which hate is normalized and often obscured through humor. However, even purely humorous memes provoked hateful comments, suggesting that factors beyond meme extremity, like topic sensitivity and referenced outgroups, also shape hateful follow-up communication.

title: How Definitions Shape Our Understanding of Political Influencers on Social Media
authors: Jennifer Oser, John Wagner, Nir Grinberg
abstract: Political discourse now circulates through sprawling social media networks where multiple actors wield influence in addition to traditional elites. Yet scholarly conclusions about who actually shapes that discourse diverge because leading studies operationalize “political influencer” in fundamentally different ways. To clarify the stakes of those choices—and advance more coherent theorizing—we examine six definitions that are prevalent in the literature and are rooted in audience size, elite ties, network importance, and message engagement. We then apply these distinctive definitions to a single dataset, namely a panel of 597,815 registered U.S. voters on Twitter during the 2020 presidential campaign to identify convergence and divergence across definitions. Three patterns emerge. First, conceptual boundaries matter: definitions that differ in scale rarely converge on the same influencers, confirming that different lenses reveal largely distinct influencer groups. Second, definitional emphasis reshapes the portrait of influence itself: elite-based criteria surface highly political, centrally positioned senders with compact but engaged followings, whereas follower- and engagement-based criteria net vastly larger, more heterogeneous groups that address politics only episodically. Third, upstream choices about conceptual boundaries and definitional emphases cascade downstream to the characteristics of influencers’ audiences, producing systematic shifts in followers’ age, gender, racial, and partisan characteristics. By showing how conceptual decisions impact both who counts as a political influencer and which citizens follow their messages, this study lays the groundwork for clearer conceptualization of the relevant dimensions for advancing the accumulation of knowledge on this increasingly important political phenomenon.

title: Modeling Civic Engagement in the Age of AI: A Communication Mediation Approach to AI News, Multifaceted Trust, and Participation in a Two-Wave Panel Study
authors: Seungahn Nah, Fanjue Liu, Jun Luo, Lee LaPlaca, Chris DeFelice
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes both a topic of news coverage and a force shaping the information environment, citizens must make sense of AI-related issues while evaluating machine-generated content, journalistic coverage, and institutional actors. This study applies the Orientation-Stimulus-Reasoning-Orientation-Response framework to examine how AI-related news consumption is associated with interpersonal discussion, multifaceted trust, and AI-related offline civic participation. Using two-wave panel data from U.S. adults (Wave 1 = 2,010; Wave 2 = 942), the study models AI-related news consumption across television, newspapers, online news sites, and social media as the stimulus; AI-related online and offline discussion as reasoning; trust in AI-generated news, legacy media coverage of AI, and AI-related institutional actors as reorientation; and AI-related offline civic participation as the response. Results reveal a selective communication pathway. Newspaper and social media AI news use were the most consistent predictors of AI-related discussion. Online discussion was associated with later trust in AI-generated news and legacy media coverage of AI, and trust in AI-generated news and AI-related institutional actors was associated with later offline participation. The observed indirect pathways operated through online discussion and trust in AI-generated news. These findings refine communication mediation research by showing that public engagement with AI-related issues depends on where people encounter AI news, how they discuss it, and which sources and institutions they come to trust.

title: Reshaping Belonging: National Identity Change in Post-Referendum Britain
authors: Jac M. Larner, James David Griffiths, Daniel Wincott
abstract: National identity is usually treated as a stable driver of political behaviour, yet we know little about whether it responds to major political events. We examine how two pivotal electoral events – the 2014 Scottish Independence Referendum and the 2016 EU Referendum – were associated with changes in citizens’ sense of national belonging. Using the 2014–2025 British Election Study Internet Panel, we show that both referendums precipitated significant shifts in national identification, primarily among those on the losing side. Post-referendum changes in Scotland proved temporary, but among Remain voters British identification fell substantially and remained depressed through 2025, with the gap between winners and losers widening over time. These findings suggest national identity is more event-sensitive than commonly assumed, and that divisive referendums may leave durable marks on how citizens in multinational states relate to the state by eroding shared national sentiment.

title: The Audience of Coalition Bargaining: Voter Reactions to Portfolio Allocation
authors: Ida B. Hjermitslev, Mathias Wessel Tromborg
abstract: Obtaining portfolios is one of the most important pay-offs that parties receive from getting into office. Accordingly, we know a lot about how portfolios are distributed between coalition partners, but surprisingly little about how voters react to these distributional outcomes. We address this research gap both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we argue that voters use cues from the quantitative and qualitative portfolio distributions to evaluate coalition partners’ competence in negotiations, which in turn shapes party support. Empirically, we use original experimental and panel survey data from the 2022 Danish general election. We find that voters infer negotiation competence from the number, power, and party-specific salience of the portfolios a party obtains. We also demonstrate that many voters paid attention to the real-world negotiation outcome and withdrew their support for the parties they perceived handled the negotiations less competently.

title: Turning Hazard Models Inside Out
authors: David Melamed, Jack G. R. Wippell, Eric W. Schoon, Ronald L. Breiger
abstract: Regression Inside Out (RIO) describes a set of related methods based on a decomposition of regression coefficients by individual cases. In this article, we offer three important extensions of RIO: 1) we generalize RIO to any model for which linear predictors are estimated; 2) we introduce an adapted bootstrap approach for determining whether case-level contributions differ from the baseline average contribution for cases; and 3) we describe how RIO is related to model diagnostics, particularly DFBETA. To illustrate the value added of these extensions, we apply RIO to a published example of the Cox proportional hazard model exploring factors associated with democratic durability.

title: Credible Prejudice? When and Why Mainstream Party Adoption of Far-Right Rhetoric Weakens Anti-Prejudice Norms
authors: Ali Karčić
abstract: This article examines whether mainstream political parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right and how such shifts shape anti-prejudice norms. Building on existing work, I argue that mainstream parties are particularly influential in weakening anti-prejudice norms because they possess greater normative credibility and legitimacy than far-right parties. Empirically, the article combines cross-national observational evidence with two preregistered survey experiments in Germany and Denmark. Using parliamentary speeches from six European countries between 1994 and 2022, I document rising mainstream party anti-Muslim rhetoric and its association with weaker norms against holding far-right views. The experiments provide causal evidence for the argument. In Germany, exposure to prejudiced rhetoric weakens anti-prejudice norms, but only when voiced by mainstream parties, rather than far right parties, likely due to their normative credibility and legitimacy. In Denmark, comparable effects are absent, consistent with decades of mainstream accommodation having already normalized such rhetoric. The experimental results also show that rhetoric targeting Muslims weakens anti-prejudice norms toward out-groups more broadly, suggesting spillover effects. These findings have important implications for future scholarship: when mainstream parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right, they affect not only electoral politics, but also the broader social norm environment.

title: Do Political Discussion Partners Share Policy Priorities and Policy Frames?
authors: Matthew T. Pietryka, Amber E. Boydstun, Taylor N. Carlson
abstract: To understand politics, people often rely on political discussion. Among the many ways that discussion may shape political perceptions, one possible mechanism is by promoting a shared sense of priorities— which issues are important. A second mechanism is by framing how people think about important issues. We examine these potential mechanisms by answering the descriptive question: Do policy priorities and policy frames tend to co-occur within political discussion networks? We answer this question by reanalyzing the 1996 Indianapolis-St. Louis Study in which participants—and their discussion partners—described the most important problem facing the United States in their own words. We show that the modal outcome is for people to hold both different priorities and different frames than their discussion partners. This finding stands in contrast to network scholarship suggesting that homophily is so often the norm. Yet we also show that people disproportionately share the same policy priorities as their discussion partners, and adopt the same frames in thinking about policy topics, especially when their policy priorities match. This finding suggests that some policy priorities are so embedded in certain frames of thinking that the topic and frame stay linked even as the topic may diffuse through a social network.

title: From Antagonistic Talk to Cooperative Acts: The Effect of Polarization Cues on Newspaper Audiences
authors: Mike Farjam, Hendrik Meyer
abstract: Do media depictions of a ‘polarized society’ merely describe division or actually deepen it? We report two laboratory experiments in Germany (Study1 $$N=302$$ ; Study2 $$N=295$$ ). After reading authentic newspaper articles in which brief polarization cues were experimentally included versus omitted, participants (i) completed standard affective- and ideological-polarization measures and (ii) played incentivized Dictator, Ultimatum, and Trust Games with ideological out-group partners. Polarization cues increased both affective polarization and ideological extremity. Behavioral responses, however, were mixed. In the Dictator Game, where the recipient cannot respond, treated participants shared less with the out-group. In the Trust Game, characterized by mutual dependence and potential efficiency gains, treated participants sent more to out-group partners. Ultimatum behavior, where interdependence is partial, showed weaker and less consistent shifts. Taken together, polarization cues reliably heighten perceived division but do not uniformly translate into behavioral antagonism: even after cues that increase self-reported polarization, participants can still cooperate with ideological opponents when cooperation is perceived as mutually beneficial.

title: Partisans misperceive and are influenced by dynamic norms
authors: Trystan Loustau, Ashley Fabrizio, Liane Young, Jordan Wylie, Stylianos Syropoulos
abstract: Perceptions of social norms, and how those norms change over time, play a central role in shaping how people understand and respond to political divides. We developed and iteratively refined dynamic‐norm messages about bipartisan attitude change to reduce divisive outparty perceptions and attitudes in a US context. We first identified real‐world issues that gained support over time among both Democrats and Republicans and were judged as believable. Study 1 documented systematic misperceptions of attitude change across a range of social issues and linked these misperceptions to colder outparty feelings. We then tested intervention messages that adapted standard static‐norm templates with the addition of information about change over time (dynamic norm; Study 2). This intervention increased expectations of future common ground but did not reliably improve downstream outparty attitudes. Next, we tested a refined intervention message that isolated dynamic norm information (Study 3). The refined dynamic norm message increased expected common ground and expected future feelings of belonging among the outparty and was associated with small but reliable increases in outparty warmth and positive outparty impressions relative to control. These results suggest that emphasizing trajectories of public opinion without highlighting current partisan gaps may be a useful strategy for reducing polarization.

title: Information Content in Text and Voice Response Formats for Open-Ended Survey Questions
authors: Camille Landesvatter, Paul C Bauer
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology
abstract: Open-ended survey questions provide valuable data alongside closed-ended questions, but they can be challenging for respondents, leading to decreases in response quality. Our study explores how survey researchers can design open-ended questions to improve response quality and yield more informative answers. In particular, we examine the effect of requesting respondents to answer questions via voice input compared to text input. We use a US sample and questions adapted from popular social survey programs. By experimentally varying the response format, we examine which format produces answers with a higher amount of information. Our findings show that spoken responses tend to be longer and also slightly more informative in terms of entropy than written responses. We also identify sociodemographic and interview context-related factors that may influence the effectiveness of voice formats in certain settings.

title: Voting for Democracy? Testing Political-Cultural Constraints on Democratic Backsliding
authors: Christopher Claassen
abstract: Democratic backsliding continues to pose a clear danger to contemporary democracies. While a growing literature shows that voters often tolerate antidemocratic candidates when partisan or ideological incentives pull in that direction, we know less about whether support for democracy, institutional trust, political tolerance, and other democratic orientations ameliorate such temptations. We address this question with a systematic comparison of six measures of political culture as predictors of electoral resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Using candidate-choice conjoint experiments fielded in three democracies facing backsliding pressures—the United States, Poland, and South Korea—we find that several democratic orientations are associated with greater resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Among them, support for the core institutions and processes of liberal democracy stands out as the most consistent predictor. Its relationship with prodemocratic choice remains meaningful even in “cross-pressured” choices where partisan or ideological incentives pull voters away from the prodemocratic option. These findings suggest that political culture matters for democratic resilience, though some components of it matter much more consistently than others.

title: Leveraging Structural Information to Reconstruct Hidden Nodes in Propagation Graphs
authors: Damian Frąszczak
abstract: While widely used for information exchange, social media networks are increasingly exploited to spread rumors and malicious content. It is essential to reconstruct propagation graphs to hold nodes accountable for such propagation. However, the dynamic and vast nature of social networks makes this task challenging. This study introduces Structural Hidden Node Identification (SHNI), a heuristic method for reconstructing partially observed propagation snapshots by identifying likely hidden participants. SHNI relies on the observed active nodes and structural neighborhood information, without requiring temporal traces, message content, user attributes, or network-specific supervised retraining; its structural parameters may be selected by expert knowledge or calibrated once and then reused across networks. Instead of materializing the entire graph in advance, the method supports on-demand neighborhood expansion from observed active nodes toward structurally relevant candidate nodes. It combines local activation pressure with a structural bridging component inspired by sociological principles of opinion formation, including local social influence, information bubbles, and the role of bridging nodes between groups. SHNI explores candidate hidden nodes through a priority-driven neighborhood expansion strategy, in which the most promising candidates are evaluated first, and further exploration stops when the heuristic evidence becomes insufficient. Experiments across different network structures show that SHNI achieves competitive reconstruction quality while maintaining low data requirements and transparent decision logic. These results indicate that SHNI is especially useful as an interpretable structural baseline when temporal traces, message content, or network-specific supervised training data are unavailable. The method may also be adapted to other propagation phenomena, such as epidemic spread or malware diffusion in computer networks.

title: Rethinking Scale: The Efficacy of Fine-Tuned Open-Source LLMs in Large-Scale Reproducible Social Science Research
authors: Marcello Carammia, Stefano Maria Iacus, Giuseppe Porro
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are distinguished by their architecture, parameter size, and performance capabilities. Social scientists have increasingly adopted LLMs to automate high-dimensional text classification tasks which are difficult to scale with human coders. Very large, closed-source models often deliver superior performance. However, reliance on large proprietary models raises concerns about transparency, reproducibility, and costs that make them impractical for large-scale research projects. In contrast, open-source models offer distinct advantages: they can be run locally (ensuring data privacy), fine-tuned for specific tasks, shared within the research community, and integrated into reproducible workflows. On the other hand, open-source models often underperform compared to commercial alternatives. In this study, we assess whether small, open-source LLMs – when fine-tuned appropriately – can match or exceed the performance of commercial alternatives such as GPT-4, while remaining feasible for large-scale academic research. To produce the labeled data that fine-tuning requires, we develop a hybrid annotation workflow in which several LLMs propose labels that human reviewers verify; this infrastructure is what makes fine-tuning feasible at scale. We apply this pipeline to three substantive social science classification tasks: coding tweets for human flourishing indicators, classifying European Parliament questions by policy area, and tagging datasets from the Harvard Dataverse. Our results show that fine-tuned models as small as Llama2-7B achieve performance on par with much larger closed models, offering a reproducible, low-cost alternative for computational social science research. We also explore the limits of fine-tuning effectiveness across model sizes and training set volumes. This work demonstrates a scalable and replicable approach to integrating open-source LLMs into empirical social science workflows.

title: Stay Healthy for Your (Our) Community: Examining How Source Identity Affects Black Americans’ Responses to Targeted COVID-19 Messages
authors: Evava S. Pietri, Veronica Derricks, India R. Johnson, Sheba M. Aikawa
abstract: Many communications during the pandemic emphasized COVID-19’s disproportionate impact on Black Americans. Articles highlighting such racial health disparities can act as a form of health information targeting , which can be threatening when aimed at marginalized identities. In Study 1, Black participants indicated a greater level of anger and distrust when reading a targeted article from a White male doctor, focusing on racial health disparities during the pandemic, compared to a non-targeted article. Source distrust was associated with decreased message persuasiveness and intentions to engage in safety behaviors. Moreover, a Black male doctor was generally more persuasive, mitigating the adverse effects of message targeting on source trust. Replicating these findings in Study 2, a Black male doctor/source was more persuasive than a White female doctor among Black women participants. Interestingly, perceptions of source bias and expertise showed a different pattern than trust, demonstrating the distinct link between distrust, targeted messaging, and threat.

title: Causal Evidence for the Role of Respect Norms in Promoting Tolerance
authors: Lucía Estevan-Reina, Marcin Bukowski, Laura Frederica Schäfer, Anna Potoczek, Dominika Gurbisz, Oliver Christ
abstract: Promoting social norms can be a powerful tool to deal with the intolerance that threatens our societies. This research explores how equality-based respect norms foster intergroup tolerance. We developed an experimental paradigm manipulating equality-based respect norms within social media to promote tolerance toward the LGBTIQ+ community in Poland. Across three studies (Study 1: N = 98; Study 2: N = 381; Study 3: N = 377), manipulations consistently affected perceptions of descriptive and injunctive norms in a Facebook post and in Polish society. Moderation analyses showed that the effect of our manipulation on tolerance emerged only among participants with less positive attitudes toward homosexual people (Study 1) or stronger disapproval of same-sex marriage (Study 3). This supports the conceptualization of tolerance as respecting others despite disapproving of their behavior. We discuss the implications of this research for the promotion of respect norms and tolerance as a way to deal with the challenges associated with divisions in society.

title: Bridging the Political Divide: Meta-Humanization and Moral Emotions Shape Partisan Reconciliation
authors: Melissa Pavetich, Sofia Stathi
abstract: In an era of deepening political polarization, understanding how partisans believe they are perceived by ideological opponents is critical for explaining both hostility and conciliation. Across five studies ( N = 1,541) conducted in the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, we examine how meta-humanization, perceiving that one’s political ingroup is seen as fully human by the outgroup, shapes moral emotional responses and downstream intergroup attitudes. Specifically, we test anger, disgust, and empathy as parallel mediators linking meta-humanization to affective polarization, negotiation, teamwork, and willingness for out-party contact, while examining perceived threat to social cohesion as a moderator. Across studies, meta-humanization reliably predicts more conciliatory intergroup attitudes, with disgust emerging as the primary affective pathway. Our findings advance theory on meta-perceptions by demonstrating that meta-humanization shapes political attitudes through moral emotion regulation, and by identifying threat to social cohesion as a condition that, under moderate levels, drives these processes. Implications for understanding and mitigating identity-based conflicts in polarized political climates are discussed.

title: The Media Bias Detector: A framework for annotating and analyzing the news
authors: Samar Haider, Amir Tohidi, Jenny S. Wang, Timothy Dörr, David M. Rothschild, Chris Callison-Burch, Duncan J. Watts
abstract: News organizations introduce bias into their coverage via the choices they make about which topics to cover (or ignore) and how to frame the issues they do decide to cover. Here, we introduce the Media Bias Detector, a scalable computational framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) with near-real-time news scraping to extract structured annotations, including political lean, tone, topics, article type, and major events, across hundreds of articles per day. We quantify these dimensions of coverage at the sentence level, the article level, and the publisher level, expanding the ways in which researchers can analyze selection and framing bias in the modern news landscape. We also release an interactive web platform for convenient exploration of these data and an accompanying dataset covering more than 140,000 articles published in 2024 by 10 prominent publishers. Last, we present some results derived from this dataset that illustrate how the MBD can uncover correlates of bias in news coverage.
